contents.name: 1.15 cotangent filtration quotients under localization
contents.support: The lemma identifies A/m^n with A_m/(mA_m)^n and induces m^r/m^n ≅ (mA_m)^r/(mA_m)^n. The assigned case is n=r+1; the local proof records an explicit inverse-residue lift.

contents.name: §4a Definition 4.1: tangent spaces to plane curves
contents.support: For a squarefree plane-curve equation, the tangent is the line cut out by the gradient when at least one partial is nonzero and is the full plane when both vanish. This is dimension-one classical support only.

contents.name: 4.22 tangent space from equations
contents.support: Milne Definition 4.22 defines the classical algebraic-set tangent by the differentials of all equations in I(V) and explicitly proves that a generating list suffices by the product rule (printed pp.86–87/PDF p.86, web lines 4578–4635). Milne assumes algebraically closed k and uses the reduced algebraic-set ideal; the assigned arbitrary-field scheme-ideal extension is proved in the linked item.

contents.name: 4.23 regular point and rank discussion
contents.support: Milne §4d, Definition 4.23 and the Jacobian tangent-rank discussion, gives dim T_aX=n-rank J(a) and the nonsingularity criterion for classical algebraic sets over algebraically closed k. §4i, Corollary 4.45, identifies nonsingularity with local-ring regularity under the classical variety conventions. These passages support the reduced classical rational-point case only; the arbitrary scheme-ideal and nonrational perfect-field cases are proved from the declared cotangent and differential suppliers.

contents.name: 4.24 differential and chain rule
contents.support: Milne proves the affine ambient differential by the Jacobian and polynomial chain rule, then shows it preserves tangent spaces of embedded classical varieties. The present item independently gives the scheme-level stalk-map construction, identity, and composition arguments; Milne’s global algebraically closed-field and classical-variety conventions are not used to enlarge the claim.

contents.name: 4.25 dual-number definition
contents.support: Milne defines the tangent space of an affine algebraic variety at P as the fibre V(k[epsilon])→V(k). This is a classical finite-type specialization under the book-wide algebraically closed-field convention; the item proves the same fibre description for any k-scheme and any k-rational point.

contents.name: 4.26 Taylor comparison
contents.support: Milne Proposition 4.26 expands equations at a classical reduced variety point and identifies its equation-defined tangent with based dual-number points (printed p.90/PDF p.89, web lines 4824–4865). Its source scope is narrower than this theorem; the linked item derives the expansion for arbitrary k and the actual scheme ideal.

contents.name: 4.27 tangent points as local dual-number maps
contents.support: For an affine variety, Proposition 4.27 identifies tangent vectors with local k-algebra maps from the local ring to k[epsilon], extending the coordinate-ring map uniquely because elements outside the point ideal map to units. This is the classical affine specialization; the item proves the local-chart construction for arbitrary k-schemes.

contents.name: 4.28 derivation
contents.support: Definition 4.28 fixes the k-derivation and Leibniz convention used by the item. Milne's surrounding argument assumes a local k-algebra with residue field k; the item verifies the coefficient derivation and module action through evaluation at the rational point.

contents.name: 4.29 local algebra comparison
contents.support: Supports the linked statement and its explicit proof route; extensions and hypothesis corrections are identified in the batch notes.

contents.name: 4.30 comparison diagram
contents.support: The diagram records Milne's canonical affine-variety identifications among the dual-number fibre, derivations, and cotangent duals, including the localization comparison. The item proves the rational-point case for an arbitrary k-scheme directly.

contents.name: 4.30(d) cotangent-space localization comparison
contents.support: Part (d) states that m_P/m_P^2 -> n_P/n_P^2 is the isomorphism of Lemma 1.15. It identifies the assigned r=1 case with intrinsic cotangent-space localization; the item proves the stronger filtration-quotient claim directly.

contents.name: §g associated-graded localization observation
contents.support: Milne states that for A=B_m and n=mA, gr(A)=direct-sum m^i/m^(i+1), citing Lemma 1.15. This records the associated-graded consequence of the filtration-quotient isomorphisms proved here.

contents.name: 4.31 functoriality
contents.support: Milne identifies the differential on classical affine-variety dual-number fibres with precomposition by the local pullback and the dual of the maximal-ideal quotient map. The item proves that compatibility for arbitrary k-schemes at rational points using the earlier dual-number lemma.

contents.support: Milne §4g is under the book-wide algebraically closed-field convention and takes a reduced algebraic set with its vanishing ideal. Its explicit warning/example supports the failure of an arbitrary displayed generator list, but does not supply the arbitrary-field, possibly nonreduced scheme statement; AG10 10.69–10.70 has that broader scope.

contents.name: 4.34 associated graded presentation
contents.support: Proposition 4.34 identifies the initial-ideal quotient with the associated graded local ring in Milne's classical algebraically closed-field setting for an algebraic set. It is only the reduced classical specialization here; AG10 10.69–10.70 permits closed algebraic subschemes and is the source with the assigned claim's arbitrary-field hypotheses.

contents.name: 4.35 regular point definition
contents.support: Milne's Definition 4.35 is specifically for points of a classical affine algebraic variety: nonsingular means lying on one irreducible component and having tangent dimension equal to that component's dimension. It supplies the classical terminology only; the assigned item defines absolute regularity for arbitrary locally Noetherian scheme points by their local rings.

contents.name: 4.44–4.45 classical local-ring criterion
contents.support: Theorem 4.44 relates minimal generators of a classical point's local maximal ideal to nonsingularity on an irreducible variety; Corollary 4.45 states nonsingular iff the local ring is regular for classical varieties. These source hypotheses are narrower than the assigned arbitrary locally Noetherian scheme statement, whose tangent-dimension equivalence is derived from the intrinsic tangent definition and finite-dimensional duality.

contents.name: 4.36 local generators criterion
contents.support: Proposition 4.36 is used inside Milne’s proof of the following classical closed-point estimate: it isolates a nonsingular point by d local generators, while the adjacent argument handles a possibly singular point. The current theorem does not rely on it for arbitrary schemes.

Its official solution reduces to affine varieties, writes the product ideal as the sum of the two equation ideals, and observes that the tangent equations split by factors. This is a classical algebraically closed-field argument; the item proves the stronger arbitrary-field scheme statement directly from based dual-number maps and the tensor coproduct formula.

contents.support: Proposition 4.29 and item 4.30 identify the classical tangent at a point with the dual of m/m^2 under the stated residue-field-equals-k hypothesis. This supports the rational-point specialization only; it does not assert the same identification at nonrational scheme points.

contents.name: §4d Definitions 4.22–4.23 and the hypersurface Jacobian criterion
contents.support: Defines the affine classical tangent via the ideal I(V), identifies its dimension as n−rank Jac, and states for a hypersurface that nonsingularity is equivalent to at least one partial derivative being nonzero. Source scope is the classical algebraically closed-field convention.

contents.name: §4h Definition 4.35: component-sensitive nonsingularity
contents.support: Defines a point as nonsingular when it lies on one irreducible component and tangent dimension equals that component dimension; otherwise singular. This supports the classical notion, not the arbitrary-scheme extension.

contents.name: 10.58 regular local rings
contents.support: For a Noetherian local ring, Milne defines regularity by equality of Krull dimension and the minimal number of maximal-ideal generators, then uses Nakayama to identify that minimum with dim_k(m/m^2). The item independently verifies that a locally Noetherian scheme has a Noetherian local stalk and identifies dim of its intrinsic tangent dual with this embedding dimension.

contents.name: 10.59 regular point from its local ring
contents.support: Milne defines a point of an algebraic scheme over k to be regular when its local ring is a regular local ring. The item adopts this absolute local-ring definition for any locally Noetherian scheme and proves the intrinsic tangent-dimension characterization directly.

contents.name: 10.59 regular scheme

contents.name: 10.60 tangent dual points and base change
contents.support: For an algebraic scheme over an arbitrary field and a point with residue field k, Milne identifies the dual-number fibre with derivations of the local ring and the dual of m/m^2. This supports the rational-point claim; the assigned item supplies the affine-neighborhood proof extending it to arbitrary k-schemes.

contents.name: 10.54–10.56 Krull and irreducible-scheme dimension
contents.support: 10.54 defines Krull dimension by prime-chain lengths; 10.56 states that the dimension of an irreducible algebraic scheme equals the dimension of its local ring at every point. This supports the local dimension of each irreducible component used after the local prime-chain comparison.

contents.name: 10.62 Jacobian
contents.support: Items 10.61–10.64 give the classical rational-point tangent-dimension/regularity comparison and Jacobian-minor description for irreducible algebraic schemes. Their stated scope does not provide the arbitrary nonreduced quotient or finite-separable nonrational residue proof; this item derives those cases locally.

Under the Axiom of Choice, for k algebraically closed of characteristic 0 and X a nonempty smooth projective classical variety over k of pure dimension d: (1) for 0<=r<=d and positive degrees e_1,...,e_r, there is a nonempty Zariski-open U in the product Pi_r = P(S_{e_1}) x ... x P(S_{e_r}) of hypersurface parameter spaces (Pi_0 = Spec k for the empty tuple) such that every closed point of U, equivalently every classical parameter, gives a nonempty scheme-theoretic intersection Z(F_1,...,F_r) = X cap V_+(F_1) cap ... cap V_+(F_r) that is smooth over k and of pure dimension d-r; (2) for r>d there is a nonempty open U with empty intersections. No claim is made about tuples outside U, about the size or density of U, about irreducibility or connectedness of the members, or about singular X. The scheme-theoretic intersection retains non-reduced structure, and smoothness is scheme-level (def-smooth-morphism-classical).
item_backing.proof_plan: Completed proof route (steps 1.1-8.1). Step 1.1 fixes the classical-scheme dictionary, perfectness, regularity and pure dimension d; 1.2 shows Pi_r is a nonempty classical projective variety whose classical points are tuples of lines; 1.3 constructs each V_+(F) by gluing chart dehomogenizations (unit discrepancies (x_k/x_j)^e) and identifies Z(F_1,...,F_r) with Spec(A_j/(f_1,...,f_r)) on each chart; 1.4 proves the closed-point criterion kappa(x)=k via the Nullstellensatz dictionary and density of closed points. Step 2.1 disposes of r=0; 2.2 transfers Bertini through the degree-e Veronese embedding: the kernel K of F -> L_F|Y' is proper because Y is nonempty, the induced morphism P(S_e) minus P(K) -> P(W_h) is surjective and carries rational points to rational points by k-linearity, and every closed point of V = pi^{-1}(U) is good. Step 2.3 forms the universal intersection W_r cap (X x Pi_r) and proves the nonemptiness locus N_r is closed by closedness of the projective projection, so the empty-intersection locus is open. Step 3.1 drops dimension by one componentwise for a form avoiding every component (nonvanishing of a coordinate power rules out containment in I(Y_l)_e). Step 3.2 cuts the rank-defect locus B out by (N-d+r)-minors of the combined Jacobian of chart generators and dehomogenized forms; the fibre dimension of Omega_{Z(t)/k} is N - rank J_comb, so B is chart-independent closed and U'_r = Pi_r minus q(B) is open. Step 4.1 builds a good tuple by induction (2.2 + 3.1). Step 4.2 shows closed points of full-rank tuples are regular of dimension d-r: rank J_comb = N-d+r, the Jacobian-kernel theorem gives dim T_x Z(t) = d-r, and the submersion criterion applied to the chart map g: X_j -> A^r yields regularity of Z(t) at x of dimension d-r. Step 5.1 shows the good tuple lies in U'_r via a standard-smooth local presentation making Omega free of rank d-r. Step 5.2 upgrades full-rank plus nonempty to smooth over k (closed points are regular; the regular locus is open and a nonempty complement would contain a point closed in Z(t), contradicting 4.2). Step 5.3 proves claim 2: after d forms the intersection is finite, one further form avoids the finite set, and further forms are arbitrary. Steps 6.1 and 7.1 conclude pure dimension d-r and claim 1 (U_r = U'_r cap N_r contains the good tuple t_0). Step 8.1 records the boundary, choice and iff dispositions. AC is declared and used exactly through the cited AC-carrying suppliers; finite choices of charts, generating lists, components and forms add no choice principle.

item_backing.support: For the parabola C=Spec(k[x,y]/(y-x^2)) inside A^2_k over any field k and every a in k, at the k-rational point P=(a,a^2) the Jacobian row of the single equation f=y-x^2 is (-2a,1), and the Jacobian-kernel isomorphism identifies the tangent space with ker(-2a,1)={(u,2au):u in k}=k*(1,2a), a one-dimensional k-vector space, equivalently the tangent line Y-a^2=2a(X-a) through P in the translated coordinates (X-a,Y-a^2)=(u,v). The maximal ideal m=(xbar-a) is principal, generated by the local parameter xbar-a, whose class is a k-basis of the cotangent space m/m^2, isomorphic via the localization lemma to the intrinsic cotangent space C_P C and dual to T_P C, so both spaces are one-dimensional. Everything holds in every characteristic, including characteristic 2, where the row is (0,1), the tangent space is k*(1,0)={(u,0)} and the tangent line is Y=a^2.
item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) Setup: k[x,y]=k[x][y] is a commutative ring, f=y-x^2 is nonzero with y-coefficient 1, I=(f) is the principal ideal and C=Spec(k[x,y]/I), with f(P)=a^2-a^2=0 for P=(a,a^2) and evaluation kernel (x-a,y-a^2) (step 1.1). (2) The substitution homomorphism sigma:k[x,y]->k[x], x->x, y->x^2, is unique and surjective, and division by the monic y-x^2 (monic in y over k[x]) writes g=qf+r with r in k[x] and sigma(g)=r, so ker sigma=(f)=I and the first isomorphism theorem gives A=k[x,y]/I = k[x] as k-algebras, with xbar->x and ybar->x^2 (step 2.1). (3) k is a domain, so k[x] and A are domains; t=xbar-a is nonzero because x-a has x-coefficient 1, hence a nonzerodivisor (step 3.1). (4) Evaluation at P factors through A as a surjective k-algebra map delta whose kernel m is the image of (x-a,y-a^2); since ybar-a^2=(xbar-a)(xbar+a) in A, m=(xbar-a) is principal and A/m=k, so delta exhibits P as the k-rational point with maximal ideal m (step 4.1). (5) With m=(t), t=xbar-a, the product ideal m^2=(t^2), and the multiplication map A/(t)->m/m^2 is well defined, surjective and injective (A a domain and t nonzero), while A/(t)=k by the first isomorphism theorem for delta, so m/m^2=k is one-dimensional with k-basis the class [t] of the local parameter (step 5.1). (6) The Jacobian of the single generator f at P is the 1x2 matrix (-2a,1), whose kernel is {(u,2au):u in k}=k*(1,2a), one-dimensional since 1 is nonzero; the Jacobian-kernel theorem gives T_P C=ker J, and the tangent line reads v=2au, i.e. Y-a^2=2a(X-a), Milne's equation (20) for F=Y-X^2; in characteristic 2 the row is (0,1) and the kernel is k*(1,0) (step 5.2). (7) The local ring is A_m with maximal ideal n=mA_m and intrinsic cotangent space n/n^2; the cotangent-localization lemma at r=1 gives m/m^2=n/n^2=k with basis the class of the local parameter, and the tangent space is the dual, so T_P C=Hom_k(k,k)=k is one-dimensional, in agreement with ker J (step 6.1). Boundaries: C, k and the cotangent space are nonempty and nonzero; the zero cases are the vertex a=0 with tangent space k*(1,0) and tangent line Y=0, the vanishing f(P)=0, the vanishing entries -2a and 2a, and the nonzero basis class [t]; there is one equation, generator, Jacobian row, local parameter, basis class and point with dimension one rather than zero; the degenerate case is characteristic 2, where the formula v=2au collapses to v=0, and no characteristic hypothesis is used elsewhere; the parameter endpoints are a=0 and the values with 2a nonzero, and the degree endpoints of f are 1 and 2; both directions of the membership equivalence ker sigma=I and of the ideal equality m=(xbar-a) are proved; and no Axiom of Choice or dependent choice is used, every cited supplier being choice-free (steps 7.1, 8.1).

item_backing.support: For char k not 2, the nodal plane cubic C=Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3-x^2)) inside A^2_k, defined by y^2=x^2+x^3, has at the origin tangent space T_0C=k^2, multiplicity two with lowest nonzero homogeneous part y^2-x^2, and scheme-theoretic tangent cone Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2)). The leading form factors as y^2-x^2=(y-x)(y+x) with two non-proportional linear factors precisely because char k is not 2, so the cone presents the two distinct lines y=x and y=-x through the origin; the node therefore has two distinct tangent directions, each factor occurring with multiplicity one in the leading form, and no reduction is performed in computing the cone.
item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) f=y^2-x^3-x^2 has the unique monomial expansion y^2-x^3-x^2 with homogeneous parts f_2=y^2-x^2 of degree 2 and f_3=-x^3 of degree 3, and generates the principal ideal I=(f) with C=Spec(k[x,y]/(f)) a closed subscheme of A^2_k (step 1.1). (2) f is nonzero (its y^2 coefficient is 1), vanishes at the origin (no constant term), and the translated expansion t_2^2-t_1^3-t_1^2 has least nonzero homogeneous part t_2^2-t_1^2 of degree 2, so the multiplicity of f at the origin is 2 (step 2.1). (3) Evaluation at the origin has maximal kernel (x,y) and kills f, so it factors through A=k[x,y]/(f), exhibiting the origin as a k-rational point of C (step 3.1). (4) Since I=(f) is principal with f in (x,y), the initial ideal is (f_min)=(y^2-x^2) and the scheme-theoretic tangent cone is Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2)), computed with the full associated graded ring and no reduction (step 3.2). (5) The Jacobian of the single generator f at the origin is the zero 1x2 matrix, so the Jacobian-kernel theorem gives T_0C=k^2 (step 4.1); both entries vanish at the origin in every characteristic. (6) (y-x)(y+x)=y^2-x^2 by distributivity, and the two linear factors are non-proportional: a proportionality would give 1=c and -1=c by coefficient comparison in the unique expansion, hence 1+1=0 in k with 1 nonzero, contradicting char k not 2 (step 4.2). So the cone presents the two distinct lines y=x and y=-x through the origin. Boundaries: C and the cone are nonempty via the k-rational origin and the two lines; the zero cases are the zero Jacobian row with kernel k^2, the vanishing constant and linear parts of f, and the vanishing xy-coefficient; there is one equation, one Jacobian row, one cone equation and one occurrence of each linear factor; the degenerate case is exactly characteristic 2, where y^2-x^2=(y+x)^2 and the two factors collapse to a doubled line, and the hypothesis char k not 2 is used only at step 4.2 to separate them; the degree endpoints are the least nonzero degree 2 and the top degree 3; no choice principle is used (every cited supplier is choice-free and no def-axiom-of-choice dependency is declared); and no biconditional is asserted, non-proportionality being obtained from a one-directional coefficient comparison (steps 5.1, 6.1).

item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) f=y^2-x^3 has homogeneous parts f_2=y^2 and f_3=-x^3, and generates I=(f), so C=Spec(k[x,y]/(f)) is a closed subscheme of A^2_k with the origin as a k-rational point: the evaluation kernel (x,y) is maximal and contains f, so it factors through the coordinate ring (steps 1.1, 2.2). (2) The translated expansion at the origin has lowest nonzero part f_2=y^2, so mult_0(f)=2=ord_m(f) (step 2.1). (3) The Jacobian of the single equation is the row (-3x^2,2y), which is (0,0) at the origin in every characteristic, so the Jacobian-kernel theorem gives T_0C=ker(0:k^2->k)=k^2 of dimension two (step 3.1). (4) Since f lies in q=(x,y) and I=(f) is principal, the initial ideal is in_q(I)=(f_min)=(y^2), so the scheme-theoretic tangent cone is Spec(k[x,y]/in_q(I))=Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2)), the x-axis doubled (step 2.3); the degree-one part of (y^2) is zero, since every nonzero multiple of y^2 has total degree at least two (step 3.2). In the coordinate velocities of T_0C=k^2 that line spans only the one-dimensional subspace {(c,0)}: the cone retains the doubling and does not determine the tangent space (step 5.1). Boundaries: nonempty (P is a k-rational point), zero Jacobian matrix with kernel k^2 and zero degree-one part of the cone ideal, one equation and one row, the nonreduced cone retained with no reduction, the source characteristic exclusion shown unused, no choice principle, and no biconditional asserted (step 6.1).

item_backing.support: Over any field k of characteristic p>0 the ideals (x^p) and (x) of k[x] have the same reduced zero set, the origin, but the closed subscheme X_p=Spec(k[x]/(x^p)) and the reduced point X_1=Spec(k[x]/(x))=Spec k have different tangent spaces there: the Jacobian of x^p is the zero polynomial in characteristic p and correctly computes the tangent space k of the thickened point, whose local ring k[tau]/(tau^p) has dimension 0 and embedding dimension 1 and is not regular, while the reduced point is a regular point with zero tangent space. Under AC the reduced point is smooth over k and the thickened scheme is not.
item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) Division by the monic x^p gives A=k[x]/(x^p) the k-basis 1,tau,...,tau^{p-1} with tau the nonzero class of x and tau^p=0, hence the direct decomposition A=k.1+(tau) (step 2.1). (2) The constant-term map is surjective with kernel (tau), so A/(tau)=k and (tau) is maximal and prime (step 3.1); every prime contains the nilpotent tau, so (tau) is the unique prime and the unique maximal ideal, A is local with residue field k, and X_p has exactly one point (step 4.1). (3) A is a finite-dimensional k-algebra, hence Noetherian, dim A=0, and m^2=(tau^2) with m=k.tau+m^2 and tau not in m^2, so the class of tau spans m/m^2, edim A=1 and A is not regular (steps 3.2, 5.1, 5.2, 6.1); every element of A outside m is a unit by the explicit inverse sum of (-u)^j with u nilpotent, so the stalk at the closed point is A_m=A (step 5.3). item_backing.support: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let k be a field, let n>=1, and let C=Spec(k[t^n,t^{n+1},...,t^{2n-1}]) be the monomial curve carried by the subring R=k[t^n,...,t^{2n-1}] of k[t]. The ideal m=(t^n,...,t^{2n-1})R is maximal with R/m=k, so the origin is a k-rational point; the classes of t^n,...,t^{2n-1} form a k-basis of m/m^2, so dim_k T_0C=n; R is a domain with dim R=1, so C is an irreducible curve; and there is no closed immersion C -> A^{n-1}_k of k-schemes. Hence the tangent dimension of an irreducible curve is unbounded, and such a curve cannot be embedded in A^{n-1}_k.
item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) R is the image of the k-algebra map k[x_n,...,x_{2n-1}] -> k[t], x_i |-> t^i, hence a finite-type k-algebra identified with a quotient; k[t] is a domain, so R is a domain and C=Spec R is a k-scheme (step 1.1). (2) R = k.1 + span_k{t^j : j>=n} is a direct sum with unique coefficients: products of generators have degree at least n and t^j for j>=n is generated by strong induction (step 2.1). (3) The constant-coefficient map R -> k is surjective with kernel m, so m is maximal with residue field k and the origin is a k-rational point; R a domain makes the zero ideal prime, so C is irreducible (step 3.1). (4) t is integral over R as a root of X^n-t^n, and the integral elements of k[t] over R form a subring containing R[t]=k[t]; so R subset k[t] is an injective integral extension and dim R=dim k[t]=1, AC entering exactly through the integral-extension dimension theorem (step 3.2). (5) m^2 is spanned by the monomials of degree at least 2n, so m = span{t^n,...,t^{2n-1}} + m^2 is direct with n basis classes in m/m^2 (step 4.1); dually the coordinate functionals form a k-basis of T_0C, so dim_k T_0C=n (step 5.1). (6) A hypothetical closed immersion into A^{n-1}_k yields, by the AC-carrying affine quotient description, an ideal I in k[x_1,...,x_{n-1}] with C isomorphic to Z=Spec(k[x]/I) over the affine chart (step 2.2), and the point q=phi(0) lies over a tuple a with f(a)=0 for all f in I (step 4.2). (7) phi^{-1} is again a k-morphism and the identity and chain rules make d_0phi a k-linear isomorphism, so dim_k T_qZ=n; the Jacobian kernel theorem identifies T_qZ with ker J(a) inside k^{n-1}, of dimension at most n-1, and n<=n-1 is a contradiction, so no closed immersion exists (steps 6.1, 7.1). Boundaries: C is nonempty with its k-rational origin and A^0_k=Spec k is nonempty in the minimal case n=1; the zero ideal of k[t] (prime) and the zero vectors of the relevant k-vector spaces are covered; the degenerate instance n=1 gives R=k[t] with m=(t) and tangent dimension one; the degree-gap endpoint 2n-1 is the largest degree strictly below m^2; AC is declared and traced to the three named suppliers (F23 in step 2.2, F11 in step 3.1, F9 in step 3.2) while the finite generating list required by F24 is furnished choice-free; no biconditional is asserted (step 8.1).

item_backing.support: For any field k, I=(x^2,xy) in k[x,y]=k[x][y] is strictly smaller than its radical sqrt(I)=(x): the element x lies in (x) but x in I would give ax+by=1 and hence 0=1 under evaluation at the origin. Both (0,1) and (0,0) are k-rational points of X=Spec(k[x,y]/I) and of the reduced line Y=Spec(k[x,y]/(x)); the Jacobians of (x^2,xy) and of (x) have the same kernel k.(0,1) at (0,1), so T_{(0,1)}X and T_{(0,1)}Y are the same one-dimensional tangent space inside k^2 (y is a unit in the local ring at (0,1) and I and (x) agree after localisation there), while at the origin the Jacobian of I is the zero matrix so T_{(0,0)}X=k^2 strictly contains T_{(0,0)}Y=k.(0,1). The witness therefore refutes 'a nonradical ideal enlarges the tangent space at every point', works over any field and in every characteristic, retains the nilpotents of k[x,y]/I, performs no reduction, and uses no Axiom of Choice.
item_backing.proof_plan: Actual completed route. (1) Choice-free radical: for ev: k[x][y] -> k[y] with x -> 0, y -> y, the coefficients of f = sum a_j(x)y^j show ev(f) = sum a_j(0)y^j, so f in ker(ev) forces every a_j in (x) by division by the monic polynomial x; hence ker(ev) = (x). Since I is contained in ker(ev) and k[y] is a domain, sqrt(I) is contained in (x), while (x) is contained in sqrt(I) because x^2 is in I; so sqrt(I) = (x) (step 3.1, step 4.1). (2) I is strictly smaller than (x) because x does not lie in I: x = ax^2+bxy would give x(1-ax-by) = 0, hence ax+by = 1 and 0 = 1 after evaluating at the origin (step 2.2). (3) The evaluation homomorphisms at (0,1) and (0,0) kill I and (x), so by the quotient universal property and the affine anti-equivalence they are k-rational points of X and Y; properness of I and (x) comes from ker(ev_(0,1)) = (x,y-1) being maximal (step 3.2). (4) Jacobian rows (2x,0) and (y,x) give kernel k.(0,1) at (0,1) and all of k^2 at the origin, while the single row (1,0) of (x) gives k.(0,1) at both points (steps 4.2, 4.3); comparison in step 5.1. (5) Local explanation of the coincidence at (0,1): y is outside m = (x,y-1), so it is a unit of R_m and x = y^{-1}(xy) shows I R_m = (x)R_m; the affine stalk identification and the localisation-quotient isomorphism identify the local rings of X and Y at the point, and the cotangent and tangent spaces are computed from the local ring alone (step 5.2).
